public_rationale: Support applies to the finding in METR’s February–June 2025 coding study, not to a universal comparison of benchmarks with real-world coding [e1, e2]. In that trial, 16 experienced open-source developers worked on 246 real issues; allowing AI increased completion time by 19% [e1]. METR contrasted this slowdown with impressive benchmark scores [e1]. This supports a qualitative mismatch between benchmark performance and practical productivity in the studied setting [e1, e2].
limitations: The study does not establish the same mismatch across all developers, tasks or LLMs; it allows for substantial productivity gains in other coding settings [e2].
Benchmark task success and developer completion time are different measures, so these results do not quantify a gap on a common scale [e1].
The supplied passages do not identify the full set of models used in the trial [e1, e2].

The follow-up begun in August 2025 showed indications of speedup, but METR’s February 24, 2026 update described selection and time-measurement problems that limited conclusions about later tools [e3].

our_interpretation: I read the explicit reference to a new METR study as a comparison between impressive benchmark performance and substantially weaker practical usefulness in that study's coding setting.
'Markedly better' describes a meaningful qualitative mismatch; benchmark success rates and developer completion times are not interchangeable numerical measures.
The target period is February–June 2025, the period investigated by the study identified through the explicit reference. This is a historical study claim, not a claim about October 2026 tools.
This reading does not establish that the same gap holds across all developers, tasks or LLMs.

criteria.contradiction_condition: The cited research finds practical coding benefits commensurate with benchmark promise, or its reported results otherwise directly reject the asserted mismatch.

The paper studies February–June 2025 tools and experienced developers working in familiar, mature repositories. It allows that other coding settings may see substantial gains, so it does not establish a universal benchmark-to-practice gap.
